title: Process design and choosing the technology
sub: Lecture 8 + Seminar 8 · the five parts of process design, QFD, process technology, people, layout, supply network, break-even
blurb: Turn a nice idea into a process you can run, and pick the cheapest technology for every quantity, capacity jump included.
h1: Process design and choosing the technology
lede: One theory question (the five parts of process design) and one calculation (choosing the technology) of Test 2. The calculation is a straight-line drawing: two minutes by hand, and it checks whatever Excel or AI gives you.
six: **Process design** is the conceptual exercise that decides the specifics of the activities that create the product or service.
Five parts: **product/service design, process technology, people jobs and organisation, layout and flow, supply network design**.
**QFD** (house of quality) turns customer requirements into technical requirements.
Supply network: low asset specificity → **market**; high specificity and high uncertainty → **vertical integration**.
**TC = FC + VC · Q**: FC is where the line starts, VC is its slope. Crossing point Q = (FC_B − FC_A) / (VC_A − VC_B).
With capacities, watch the **jump**. Data per month instead of per year: same numbers, don't divide by 12.
foot: Sources: 3BE216 lecture and seminar slides 'Process Design' and 'Selection of Technology', practice Test 2 (exercises 3 and 4) and its answer key, Lecture and Seminar 8 as recorded.

questions.answer: the conceptual exercise that determines the specifics of the activities that create the product or service
questions.e: From the slide. First you design, then you build.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the five parts of process design?
questions.e: The five: product/service design, process technology, people jobs and organisation, layout and flow, supply network design.

questions.q: QFD (house of quality) is used to…
questions.answer: turn customer requirements into technical requirements
questions.e: The customer wants 'red'; you manufacture an RGB code you can check.

questions.answer: the steps, tools, methods and systems to obtain the output
where the workstations are and how material, products and information flow
questions.e: How the process works in the real space.

questions.q: Who should write the job description for a production role?
questions.e: From the lecture: HR polishes and publishes it, but you know what the job needs.

questions.q: Very specific material, and nobody on the market makes it (high specificity, high uncertainty). What do you do?
wrong: Sign a contract with any supplier
questions.e: High asset specificity and high uncertainty → vertical integration.

questions.q: A simple item that many suppliers sell (low asset specificity). What do you do?
questions.answer: Buy it on the market (market transaction)
questions.e: Low asset specificity → market transaction, whatever the uncertainty.

questions.q: In TC = FC + VC · Q, the fixed cost is…
questions.answer: where the line starts on the cost axis

questions.q: CNC-A: FC 2.7 M, VC 240. CNC-B: FC 3.6 M, VC 210. Where do they cost the same?
Same machines: you need 35 000 units. Which CNC?
questions.e: Above 30 000 the flatter line (lower VC) is cheaper.

questions.q: B is cheapest up to 7 600 but can only make 5 000. A is cheaper than C up to 6 000. For 5 500 units?
questions.e: The jump: B no longer exists, compare A and C → A up to 6 000.

questions.q: The same cost table is given per month instead of per year. What changes?
questions.answer: Only the unit: the intervals are now per month
questions.e: Same numbers, per month. Don't divide by 12.

questions.q: Two options have the same variable cost. What do you choose?
questions.answer: The one with the lower fixed cost, at every quantity
wrong: The one with the higher capacity

questions.q: Suppliers I (FC 10 000, VC 400), II (30 000, 200), III (40 000, 150). Cheapest for 150 pieces, no capacities?
questions.e: I up to 100, II from 100 to 200, III above 200. The I/III crossing at 120 doesn't matter: it is above II.

questions.q: You need thousands of identical metal parts. CNC or 3D printing?
questions.answer: CNC: 3D printing is still much slower for big volumes
wrong: Either, the time is the same
questions.e: From the lecture: one part in 15 min on a CNC can take 3 hours printed.

vocab.meaning: The conceptual exercise deciding the specifics of the activities that create the output.
Decides the output of the process.
The steps, tools, methods and systems that obtain the output.
Organisational structure, job descriptions and profiles, coordinated with HR.
Where the workstations are and how material and information flow.
The operation in the context of its suppliers and customers.
Quality function deployment, the house of quality: customer requirements → technical requirements.
Computer numerical control: a machine tool run by a computer program.
Customer relationship management: learning and keeping customer needs to reach the highest profit.
Owning the supplier (upstream) or the route to the customer (downstream).
How specific the thing you need is.
Cost that doesn't depend on the quantity: the start of the line.
Cost per unit: the slope of the line.
The quantity where two options cost the same.

facts: QFD turns customer requirements into {technical|financial|legal|marketing} requirements.
A 3D printer for metal is still much {slower|faster|cheaper|bigger} than a CNC for big volumes.
Low asset specificity means you buy it on the {market|contract|factory|stock}.
In TC = FC + VC · Q the variable cost is the {slope|start|end|crossing} of the line.
CNC-A and CNC-B cost the same at {30000|25000|35000|50000} units.
Data per month instead of per year: do not divide by {12|2|100|52}.
